concept.name: Skewness
concept.definition: A measure of the asymmetry of a distribution about its mean, defined as the third standardized moment. Zero indicates symmetry, positive values indicate a longer right tail, and negative values a longer left tail.
concept.intuition: It tells you which side the surprises live on: negatively skewed returns have occasional large crashes amid small gains; positively skewed returns have occasional large wins amid small losses.
concept.mechanics: Average the cubed deviations from the mean and divide by the cube of the standard deviation; cubing preserves sign, so the heavy tail determines the sign. Software typically reports the sample-size-adjusted Fisher-Pearson coefficient, with the correction factor approaching 1 for large N.
concept.formula: g1 = [SUM_{i=1..N}(Y_i - Y_bar)^3 / N] / s^3, where Y_bar is the mean and s is the standard deviation computed with N in the denominator; adjusted version G1 = [sqrt(N(N-1))/(N-2)] * g1.
concept.failure_modes: Sample skewness is extremely sensitive to outliers - NIST's Cauchy example yields a sample skewness of 70 from a symmetric distribution - and multimodality can flip its sign, so it cannot be read at face value without a histogram. It is also undefined when the third moment does not exist.
concept.misconceptions: Skewness zero does not prove normality (many non-normal distributions are symmetric), and the sign describes the tail, not where most of the mass sits - a right-skewed distribution typically has most observations below its mean.
concept.example: Daily equity-index returns commonly show skewness around -0.3 to -1, quantifying the crash-prone left tail that a symmetric normal model would miss.
